stories.headline: The Wrong Number
stories.dek: The league will vote on a third IR slot, and all summer both sides argued it by counting how many teams have a full IR. That number does not measure what a slot costs.
stories.why: The vote is real, it is coming, and the finding is strong enough to decide it. It should carry a name, not read as desk output.
stories.angle: Both camps counted the same wrong quantity. Teams at cap is 9 of 16. Constrained teams — IR full AND still holding an injured man, the only state in which a manager would actually use a new slot — is 5. Four teams sit at 2/2 with nobody to move; give them a slot and they sign nobody. Counting the two together overstates the cost of expansion by 1.8x.

sections.note: The mechanism, and it is the thing the whole summer went past. A Sleeper IR slot does not hold a man who would otherwise be a free agent — it holds somebody already on your roster and frees an ACTIVE spot, which gets filled off the wire immediately. So the cost of a slot is the healthy replacement, not the injured player. One man out of the pool per slot actually used.

Four weeks, taken automatically every Wednesday, never edited after. Constrained went 1 → 1 → 4 → 5; injured men parked on active rosters went 3 → 13. The point to land: it was flat for the first two weeks. A vote taken in August was voting on the flat part.
The counting error, with all sixteen rosters printed so anyone can check it.

sections.h: What it would cost the wire
sections.note: A third slot: 5 players off a 506-man pool, 0.99%. A fourth: 6, 1.19%. The difference between the two proposals is one player and one team, because only one manager in the league is holding more than one injured man on an active roster.

sections.h: The ones not using what they have
sections.note: Five teams are under the current cap while carrying an injured player. The slot they are voting on is a slot they already own and have not filled. Awkward for both sides — Smoke Dragons is on that list.
Three is cheap and the case strengthens on its own if the trend holds. Four is not worth a second ballot.

stories.figures: Do not hand-type any number. scripts/build_ir.py reads ir-watch.json and generates all three figures plus the share card; re-running it after a new week re-types them. Write the prose around the figures, not over them.
stories.deskVersionNote: A desk-written version already exists and is published. It is the skeleton, not the piece — John's version replaces it under his byline.

stories.headline: Two Leagues
stories.dek: The chat and the standings are separate universes. Who you argue with has almost nothing to do with who you play.
stories.why: Pitched during the heat work and never started. The evidence is already gathered.
stories.angle: The heat grid and the results table describe two different leagues living in the same sixteen franchises. Rivalry in the chat does not track rivalry on the field — not by schedule, not by record, not by playoff meetings.

sections.note: Put the heat grid and the head-to-head grid side by side and look at how little they rhyme.
The hottest pairings, and what those same pairs have actually done to each other on the field.
The real rivalries by result — close games, playoff meetings, swings — and how quiet most of them are in the chat.
Proximity, history and politics, none of which the schedule knows about.
